//: Metadata for the patch-package patches in this directory — one key per patched npm package. Consumed by the orphaned-patch guard (packages/dev-tools/patch-reconcile/check-patches.mjs, run as `npm run lint:patches`) and the renovate-patch-reconcile workflow. Every patches/<pkg>+<version>.patch MUST have an entry here with a matching patchedVersion. When a patch is removed, delete its entry. See patches/README.md.

@zenfs/core.reason: #2146: VCache.ref coalesced DIFFERENT paths onto one vnode when their inodes shared an ino (poisoned indexes carry many ino-0 entries) — the shared inode object cross-stamps size/mode between unrelated files. The patch refuses cross-path coalescing unless the inodes are a genuine hardlink: ino must be nonzero, format bits must match, AND nlink must be > 1 on both sides (#2034). A duplicated real ino with nlink 1 is a poisoned index, not a link — and because every vnode also owns its sparse data cache, two colliding paths open at once returned each other's bytes (8 parallel preview fetches all served the entry file; sequential reads evicted the vnode between calls and were correct). ALSO (zen-fs/core#312): Index._alloc() computed the next inode id as Math.max(...[...this.values()].flatMap(i => [i.ino, i.data])) — a single spread of 2x entryCount arguments. _alloc() is called by IndexFS.create(), which backs createFile/createFileSync/mkdir/mkdirSync, so EVERY file and directory creation on the OPFS backend (WebAccessFS extends Async(IndexFS)) paid it; past the host's spread-argument ceiling the engine throws RangeError('Maximum call stack size exceeded') and nothing can be created on the mount again. The ceiling is really arguments-vs-remaining-stack, so it is not a clean cliff: measured in a live Chrome 151 kernel worker the shallow-stack ceiling bisected to 63,551 arguments (31,775 entries), while the production index of 26,013 entries (52,026 arguments) survived ~800 extra frames and threw at ~1,000 — an intermittent write failure that grew more frequent as the VFS did. The patch replaces the spread with a reduction, which also drops the per-creation O(n) array allocation. Only behavioral difference: an EMPTY index yields 1 instead of -Infinity, and IndexFS.create requires the parent entry to exist so it can never reach _alloc on an empty index.
@zenfs/core.removeWhen: Local workaround — no upstream PR is tracked. Remove once @zenfs/core refuses to share a vnode across paths for non-hardlink inodes upstream. (The patch also used to rewrite `globalThis.__zenfs__` into an own-property copy so a probe could enumerate it; upstream declined that in https://github.com/zen-fs/core/issues/310 — the global is deliberately minimal — so that hunk is gone and consumers must probe by existence plus the `_version` export instead.) The _alloc() spread hunk goes once zen-fs/core#312 ships.
@zenfs/core.verify: npm run test -w @slicc/webapp -- zenfs-ino-collision-patch virtual-fs-concurrent-read zenfs-alloc-overflow-patch

@zenfs/dom.reason: WebAccessFS.write opened every write with createWritable({ keepExistingData: true }), so Chromium copied the whole existing file into the swap file first — O(file size) per write even when the write replaces the file (92 MB rewrite: 480ms -> 240ms without the copy). Worse, IndexFS.touch only narrows the in-memory inode and nothing truncates the handle, so a shrink left its tail on disk forever (92 MB file rewritten as 4 MB kept 92 MB of OPFS quota). The patch keeps the copy only where the write needs it: a non-zero offset, or a buffer that does not span the indexed size. ALSO (#2146): WebAccessFS minted ino:0 inodes in stat's ENOENT recovery and _loadMetadata's reality branch; thousands of ino-0 index entries collapse onto one VFS vnode-cache slot, stamping one file's size/mode onto another path on sync (phantom directories, sibling-size truncation). The patch allocates unique ino/data pairs at both sites. ALSO: those #2146 allocations must set nlink: 1 — ZenFS's Inode constructor warns on every ino!=0/nlink==0 inode and kerium retains every log entry, so leaving nlink unset flooded the in-memory log on every inode materialization until its backing Set hit V8's 2^24 cap and every FS op threw 'Set maximum size exceeded' (2026-08-18 VFS-offline incident). ALSO (#2157): a 0-byte file never reached OPFS at all — the VFS vnode only calls the backend's `write` for dirty BYTE ranges and an empty file has none, so `IndexFS.createFile` put an inode in the index and no FileSystemFileHandle was ever created. `stat`/`exists` then answered from the index while `unlink` raised ENOENT from `removeEntry`, and ZenFS clears the vnode cache only AFTER a successful unlink, so the entry reverted to existing: `rm` could not delete a 0-byte file at all, and `rm -f` / `rm -rf` reported success while deleting nothing. The patch materializes the handle in `createFile` (every indexed file then exists on disk, and the first write skips the failing lookup it used to pay for) and makes `remove` tolerate an already-absent OPFS entry — IndexFS has already validated existence against the authoritative index, so an entry it knows but OPFS does not was otherwise undeletable forever: the phantom-deletion class. The `createFile` insert is rolled back when OPFS refuses the create (quota, permission): `super.createFile` has already added the inode, so leaving it on the error path would recreate the same divergence from the other side — `stat` reporting a file that was never created, the next create hitting EEXIST, and a flush able to persist the phantom into the sidecar.
@zenfs/dom.removeWhen: Local workaround — no upstream PR is tracked. Remove once @zenfs/dom decides keepExistingData per write (or truncates the handle on a narrowing touch) AND materializes a backing handle for empty files upstream.

kerium.reason: kerium's log() retains EVERY entry in a module-global List (a plain Set underneath) with no cap or rotation — even entries below the output threshold that are never printed (default minLevel is ALERT). A long-lived kernel worker under log pressure (e.g. ZenFS's per-inode nlink warning) eventually hits V8's 2^24-element Set cap, after which entries.add throws RangeError('Set maximum size exceeded') into every logging caller — every ZenFS op failed and the VFS went offline (2026-08-18 incident). The patch evicts the oldest entry beyond a 10,000-entry ring so the backlog stays bounded.
kerium.removeWhen: Remove once kerium bounds its log backlog upstream (ring buffer or opt-in retention).

just-bash.reason: curl formats the response for stdout (`N(...)` → latin1 decode of the WHOLE body via `Buffer.from(body).toString('binary')`) BEFORE checking `-o`/`-O`, then discards the string. In the browser the `buffer` polyfill's latin1Slice builds that string one `+=` per byte, so every downloaded byte costs a ~32-byte V8 cons-string node: a 250 MB `curl -o` needed ~8 GB of V8 heap and crashed the leader tab (renderer OOM → Inspector.targetCrashed). The patch skips the stdout formatting when the body is going to a file (unless `-v`, which still prints it), so `curl -o` costs the body bytes, not a string copy of them.
just-bash.removeWhen: Remove once just-bash's curl only formats the body for stdout when it will be printed (or streams `-o` output to the fs).
